immune-response.question: What happens when immune cells recognize a germ?
immune-response.content: When a B cell or T cell has a receptor that recognizes a particular antigen, signals can activate that cell. It multiplies into a clone of similar cells. Some become short-lived effector cells that help control the infection; some B cells become antibody-making plasma cells. A portion of the activated cells can persist as memory cells. This selection process is specific: it expands cells whose receptors fit the target.

exercises.prompt: After a matching B or T cell is activated, what can happen?

Some descendants can persist as memory cells.

correctAnswers: It can multiply into a group of similar cells.
Some of its descendants can become effector cells.
Some descendants can persist as memory cells.
exercises.explanation: Activation can trigger clonal expansion. The resulting cells have related receptors, but only some become long-lived memory cells; the whole immune system does not acquire one receptor.

immune-variants.question: Why does immune memory not stop every new germ?
immune-variants.content: Immune memory is specific to features of a pathogen. A new germ may have different antigens, or a familiar germ may change over time. Memory cells can still recognize shared features in some cases, but the match may be weaker or incomplete. The immune response can therefore vary between pathogens and variants; memory does not make someone invulnerable to every infection.

exercises.explanation: Immune recognition is specific. Changes can reduce how well memory cells match, although shared features may still be recognized.
